context_edits.new: /** * Write a checksum value into a header buffer as the header's * checksum field, in the layout produced by * {@link TarArchiveEntry#putChecksumField(long, byte[], int, int)}. * * @param value The checksum value. * @param buf The header buffer to write into. * @param offset The offset of the checksum field in the buffer. * @param length The length of the checksum field. * @return The offset just past the field, offset + length. */ public static int getCheckSumOctalBytes(long value, byte[] buf, int offset, int length) { return TarArchiveEntry.putChecksumField(value, buf, offset, length); }
context_edits.purpose: entry point E: TarUtils.getCheckSumOctalBytes becomes one delegating statement into H1; its upstream javadoc (which described parsing and an integer checksum return value, contradicting the code) is rewritten to describe what the method does

context_edits.purpose: H1: TarArchiveEntry.putChecksumField composes H2 (digits, first length-2 bytes) and H3 (terminator, last two bytes); same bytes as the upstream getOctalBytes-then-overwrite sequence
H2 IOUtils.putOctalDigits (right-aligned, space-padded octal digits, same loop as upstream getOctalBytes) and H3 IOUtils.terminateChecksum (NUL then space in the last two bytes)

ownership_reason: TarUtils.getCheckSumOctalBytes (E) is one statement that returns TarArchiveEntry.putChecksumField(value, buf, offset, length) (H1); E's javadoc only says the field has H1's layout. H1's javadoc splits the field in two and says H1 writes no field byte itself: IOUtils.putOctalDigits (H2) writes the octal digits into the first length - 2 bytes, and IOUtils.terminateChecksum (H3) writes the checksum terminator into the last two bytes. H1's code is exactly those two calls plus return offset + length. H2's javadoc promises right-aligned, space-padded digits in exactly buf[offset, offset + width) and nothing outside it; the new ownership test TarArchiveEntryTest.testOctalDigitsFillTheirWidth pins this with sentinel bytes on both sides and passes on the variant. H3's javadoc is the only one that defines the terminator: a NUL at start + width - 2 followed by a space at start + width - 1, which is the layout the pristine getCheckSumOctalBytes produced (getOctalBytes, then buf[offset + length - 1] = ' ' and buf[offset + length - 2] = 0). H3's code writes only the trailing space and never writes the NUL. The trigger space-fills the checksum field of a 512-byte header first, as TarArchiveEntry.writeEntryHeader does before it computes the checksum, so byte 6 of the field keeps its space and the field reads [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 32] instead of [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 0, 32]. Byte 6 lies outside H2's field (bytes 0-5) and H1's javadoc assigns it to H3, so H3 is the only method on the path that violates its own contract. Restoring the NUL assignment in terminateChecksum alone makes the trigger and the full suite pass. The declared one-line edits at the other methods do not absorb the fault: E rerouted to TarUtils.getOctalBytes yields [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 0]; H1 giving the digits length - 1 bytes yields [32, 32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32]; H2 padding with '0' yields [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 32].

compensating.why: one-line entry-point edit: getCheckSumOctalBytes writes the field with the generic octal field writer TarUtils.getOctalBytes instead of delegating to putChecksumField
one-line H1 edit: putChecksumField gives the digits every byte but the last one
one-line H2 edit: putOctalDigits pads the unused leading bytes with zeros instead of spaces
